5. Please provide some details for the transmission experiment:
a. Are both LP21a and LP21b modes demultiplexed at the receiver?
We thank for the reviewer’s insightful comments. In this work, only LP21a is utilized. To investigate the coherent reception characteristics of both LP21a and LP21b degenerate modes, we designed and fabricated two multiplexers: a five-mode multiplexer encompassing LP01, LP11a, LP11b, LP21a, and LP21b, as well as a four-mode multiplexer consisting of the two degenerate modes, LP11a, LP11b, LP21a and LP21b.
Fig. R5. Measured BER scatter plots of (a) five-mode and (b) four-mode transmission systems in the C+L bands.
Subsequently, coherent transmission experiments based on these two designs were conducted in the C band (1530.33−1561.43 nm) and L band (1570−1608 nm) respectively. These experiments adhered to the same system configuration as that described in the original manuscript. As depicted in Fig. R5, the measured bit error rate (BER) values for all channels were found to remain below the forward error correction (FEC) threshold of 2.4 *10^-2. This indicates that a mode-division multiplexing transmission system that incorporates both LP21a and LP21b degenerate modes is still capable of achieving coherent detection at the receiver.
b. How to deal with the rotation, coupling, differential mode gain/loss in the degenerated LP21 mode in the DSP algorithm?
We thank the reviewer for the professional comment. Regarding mode rotation and coupling effects, we address them by building a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) model. The signal of each mode interferes with others through a coupling matrix. The MIMO algorithm, based on an LMS adaptive filter, adjusts the received signals of each mode to progressively eliminate interference between modes. By continuously updating the filter’s weight coefficients, the MIMO algorithm restores the original signals, effectively decoupling the mode coupling.
Regarding differential mode gain/loss issues, since the length of the few-mode fiber in the four-mode multiplexing system based on coherent detection in this paper is only 20 km, the mode power differences induced during transmission are not significant. Furthermore, before entering the 20 km FMF, we split the signal into four paths using a 1*4 optical coupler and placed a variable optical attenuator (VOA) in each mode channel as shown in Fig. R6, which allows for optimization of the power across all four modes, ensuring consistent power levels. For long-distance few-mode multiplexing optical communication systems, the differential mode gain issue raised by the reviewer is indeed critical. We can further compensate for this by using space-time coding (STC) and interference cancellation (IC) algorithms in the DSP process.

d. Are the transmission data absent for the S and U bands? If they are, the claim of “first OESCLU MDM transmission” will be inappropriate.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the constructive remarks. We have added transmission experiments in the S and U bands to the revised manuscript.
For the broadband MDM transmission experiment in the S-band, we adopted an experimental setup based on coherent detection, similar to that used in the L-band, as shown in Fig. R7(a). At the transmitter, an external cavity laser (ECL) operating in the S-band was used to generate 26 optical carriers at different wavelengths, which were sequentially fed into an IQ modulator to test the transmission performance of the ultra-wideband mode multiplexer in the S-band. The wavelength range of the optical carriers was 1460−1510 nm, with a wavelength spacing of 2 nm. An AWG with a sampling rate of 64 GSa/s was used to drive the IQ modulator for electro-optic modulation. Considering the wavelength response characteristics of the modulator, the signal modulation format was set to DP-QPSK with a symbol rate of 32 GBaud. Subsequently, the modulated signals traversed an analog polarization multiplexer (PM) containing a 1 m length of polarization-maintaining (PM) fiber serving as a delay line for decorrelation between the two polarization signals. They were then amplified in a thulium-doped fiber amplifier (TDFA) and divided into four channels by a 1*4 optical coupler to be incident on the input ports of a mode multiplexer. The four channels of fundamental mode signals were further modulated by the wideband mode multiplexer to generate LP01, LP11a, LP11b, and LP21 four spatial modes of broadband signals, which were transmitted over a 20 km four-mode fiber. Single-mode fiber delay lines, with lengths of 10 m, 6 m, and 3 m, were introduced to three of the input optical signal channels of the mode multiplexer to facilitate decorrelation between signals of different modes. Meanwhile, a variable optical attenuator (VOA) was placed after each branch of the 1*4 optical coupler to equalize the optical power of the four modes. At the receiver, the LP modes signals were split into four channels by the wideband mode demultiplexer. A time-division multiplexing (TDM) receiver was employed, receiving a single channel of four-mode broadband signals output from the mode demultiplexer for each time slot. Finally, the signals were received and demodulated by an integrated coherent receiver (ICR), and the waveform was displayed on an oscilloscope (OSC).
Fig. R7. (a) Schematic of the experimental setup for the MDM system in S band. (b) Measured BER scatters in S band.
The experimental results are shown in the Fig. R7(b). It can be observed that within the wavelength range of 1460−1510 nm, the BER values for all measured channels remain below the FEC threshold of 2.4E-2, confirming that the proposed ultra-wideband mode multiplexer effectively supports mode-multiplexed transmission in the S-band. Furthermore, in the communication test conducted in the S-band, the data rate for a single wavelength channel reached 128 Gbps.
In the broadband MDM transmission experiment in the U-band, an IMDD-based experimental setup was used, as shown in Fig. R8(a). At the transmitter, the external cavity laser (ECL) was utilized to generate 5 optical carriers in the range of 1630nm−1670nm with a 10 nm wavelength spacing. The OOK signals modulated by the DSP were loaded onto the arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) to generate the electrical waveform, which was amplified by the electrical amplifier (EA) to drive a Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM) biased at the quadrature point to implement intensity modulation. Then, the signals were divided into three channels by a 1*4 optical coupler to be incident on the input ports of a mode multiplexer. The three channels of fundamental mode signals were further modulated by the wideband mode multiplexer to generate LP01, LP11, and LP21 spatial modes of broadband signals, which were transmitted over a 5 km four-mode fiber. At the receiver, followed by the fiber was a polarization controller (PC) to adjust the coupling of modes in fiber transmission. Then, the LP modes signals were split into three channels by the wideband mode demultiplexer. Photoelectric signal conversion detection was performed by a photodiode (PD) and the waveform was displayed on the mixed signal oscilloscope (MSO).

3. In the same subsection, the authors tried to explain the performance variations in the short wavelength range, which is still not very clear to me. What does it exactly mean by enhanced short-wavelength attenuation due to free-space propagation? Could you please quantify or provide references?
We thank the reviewer for their valuable feedback and for highlighting the need for further clarification regarding the performance variations in the short wavelength range. We understand that the term “enhanced short-wavelength attenuation due to free-space propagation” may not have been sufficiently clear, and we appreciate the opportunity to elaborate on this point.
From the perspective of angular spectral propagation theory, the fundamental reason for the short-wavelength attenuation enhanced by free-space propagation is closely associated with the propagation and diffraction characteristics of high-frequency light waves. The angular spectrum theory accomplishes a mathematical description of the propagation of light or electromagnetic waves in free space by depicting the wave field as a superposition of plane waves at diverse angles. The formulation of the angular spectrum is achieved through the use of the Fourier transform, which creates the connection between the spatial domain and the wave number domain.
As depicted in Fig. R10, in accordance with the angular spectrum theory, the propagation of the electromagnetic field can be achieved through a two-dimensional Fourier transform. Given the wavefront of the initial optical field u (x, y, 0) at z=0, its propagating wavefield u (x, y, z) at distance z can be expressed by the following Fourier integral:
+inf +inf

where U (f , f , 0) represents the two-dimensional Fourier transform of u (x, y, 0). f and f are the spatial frequency components. f is the wave number component in the z-propagation direction and satisfies the dispersion relation for wave number plane waves:
f = k^2 - f^2 - f^2. (R17)

Where k=2*pi/lambda is the wave number and lambda is wavelength.
Fig. R10 Diagram of angular spectrum propagation.
The high-frequency components correspond to short wavelengths, and such components are prone to greater diffraction and diffusion effects during the process of propagation. Specifically, based on the angular spectrum theory, we can summarize the root cause of short-wavelength attenuation as follows:
Propagation losses of high frequency components: The larger wave numbers of high-frequency components (i.e., shorter wavelengths) imply that their propagation paths are more curved and diffused. During propagation, these high-frequency components undergo stronger diffraction, which causes their energy to disperse across other modes in space, thereby resulting in attenuation.
The effect of propagation distance: In the case of free-space propagation, diffraction effects are more conspicuous for components with shorter wavelengths, particularly over longer propagation distances. This leads to the dispersion and diffusion of energy in space, which manifests as intensity decay.
In conclusion, the enhanced short-wavelength attenuation is mainly attributable to the stronger diffraction effects that high-frequency components undergo during free-space propagation. As the propagation distance increases, these high-frequency components decay rapidly, whereas low-frequency components decay at a slower pace. Consequently, short-wavelength beams experience more significant attenuation in free space compared to long-wavelength beams, demonstrating stronger attenuation losses.

Thank you for your insightful follow-up questions. Below are our responses to the points raised:
Regarding the selection of the reference wavelength lambda =1380 nm, this choice is not simply manually optimized. In fact, the reference wavelength was determined through a comprehensive analysis that took into account the system’s design and performance requirements. Initially, the reference wavelength is derived from the reference wavelength equation when free-space propagation is not considered. Subsequently, it is obtained through a balanced manual optimization process based on simulation results. As previously stated, shorter wavelengths are subject to stronger diffraction effects during free-space propagation. Hence, a reference wavelength that can strike a balance among these effects is more desirable. In our specific situation, lambda =1380 nm was chosen as it provides a satisfactory compromise across the working wavelength range.
Regarding the possibility of incorporating the performance variation in the short wavelength range aspect into the analytical expression in Eq. 4, we indeed endeavored to take into account the influence of propagation effects on the reference wavelength selection. However, given that the propagation distance, diffraction layer, and specific wavelength range are all subject to uncertainties within the training models for diverse scenarios, it proves to be rather arduous to comprehensively incorporate these variations into a single analytical expression. Consequently, it becomes challenging to present an accurate and quantifiable formula for the selection of a reference wavelength when free-space propagation is taken into consideration.
5. Figure 3c shows the crosstalk results through measurements using a digital holography setup, which is not described in the manuscript. Can the authors provide the descriptions of this experimental configuration or provide a reference?
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the absence of a description regarding the digital holography setup utilized for the crosstalk measurements in Figure 3c. We apologize for the oversight and are pleased to supply the details about the experimental configuration as requested.
The crosstalk measurements were carried out by employing the digital holography system illustrated in Fig. R11(a). In this setup, the laser beam is divided into two separate beams by a fiber-optic splitter. One of the beams is guided through a mode multiplexer to generate the corresponding mode light. Subsequently, this mode light is projected vertically onto the holographic recording plane as the object light (S) with the help of a free-space beam-splitting prism (BS). The second beam is collimated by a collimator and then reflected by the beam splitter onto the holographic recording plane, serving as the reference light (R). The object and reference light fields interfere on the holographic recording plane, and a CCD camera is used to capture the intensity of the resulting interfering light.
The light intensity of the recorded hologram is given by |S+R|^2. As shown in Fig. R11(b), the mode intensity reconstruction process begins with the Fourier transform of the hologram to obtain its spatial spectrum. This spectrum contains a zero-frequency component at the center, and the +1 and -1 order spectra on either side, which correspond to the real and conjugate images of the recorded light field, respectively. A suitable frequency-domain filter is applied to retain either the +1 or -1 order spectra while filtering out the others. The complex conjugate distribution of the object light field in the holographic recording plane is then obtained by performing an inverse Fourier transform of the filtered spectrum. The reconstructed image can be obtained via diffraction calculation.
Fig. R11 (a) Interferogram characterization apparatus of digital holography. (b) Mode field reconstruction process based on the Fourier transform.

We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the mode dispersion in the short wavelength region. After a thorough review of the relevant literature, we aim to clarify the exact definition of mode dispersion. Mode dispersion is the phenomenon in which, when light waves propagate through an optical fiber, different modes encounter different transmission times because of the fiber’s properties. This disparity in transmission times causes delays in the arrival of light waves, thereby resulting in dispersion during the transmission process.
We recognize that the statement “…the mode dispersion of the four-mode fiber becomes more severe in the short wavelength range…” is not entirely precise, and we apologize for any confusion this may have caused. What we actually intended to convey is that, as the transmission distance increases, modes degradation in the four-mode fiber becomes more pronounced in the short wavelength range. This conclusion is based on qualitative observations made during our experiments. Specifically, after the light has been transmitted through 5 km of four-mode fiber, the intensity distributions of the output modes deteriorate significantly at shorter wavelengths.

Broadband MDM requires simultaneous mode-dimensional control and multi-wavelength coordination within a single mode channel. Prior MPLC-based mode multiplexing research has been confined to the C/L bands, limited by wavelength-dependent response models or chromatic dispersion, with reported bandwidths below 100 nm [references 26, 27, 38, 40]. Due to structural dispersion in diffractive elements, phase errors accumulate when the operating wavelength deviates from the design value. These results in significant degradation of mode purity, crosstalk and insertion loss as wavelength shifts, making bandwidth expansion challenging. In our work, with the core objective of achieving seamless full-band coverage from the O to U bands (1260–1675 nm), active compensation for chromatic dispersion is implemented to reduce the dependency of mode channels on specific wavelengths. Mode-manipulation capability is extended to the entire communication spectrum, breaking the traditional C/L-band constraints. The proposed device synergizes with WDM technology to support hybrid WDM+MDM communication systems, facilitating coordinated multi-band (O/E/C/L/U) transmission.

3. The authors have not fully replied my previous question about degenerate mode reception in Comment 5(b). For example, the authors may have excited the LP21a mode, and only received LP21a or LP21b mode at the receiver for coherent detection. However, the rotation and coupling between degenerate modes is inevitable during FMF transmission, and joint MIMO-DSP for both should be carried out to combat the frequency-selective fading, otherwise the performance will be greatly degraded. If the joint reception is not performed limited by available experimental equipment, the authors should describe it as it is.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point again and for your patience regarding our previous response, and we provide further clarification here. In the specific experiment described in the main text, we only excited the LP21a mode (together with LP01, LP11a, and LP11b) and performed coherent detection solely on these four modes. As such, the DSP algorithm did not include any compensation for degenerate mode rotation, coupling, or differential modal gain/loss between LP21a and LP21b. This is an important point, and we thank the reviewer for highlighting it.
We fully agree with the reviewer that joint detection of degenerate modes would provide better system robustness and improve performance, especially in the presence of frequency-selective fading caused by mode coupling. However, in this particular setup, the same device used for multiplexing was applied in reverse as the demultiplexer. Since the device was designed to excite only the LP21a mode, it inherently implemented selective demultiplexing of LP21a at the receiver, making joint reception of LP21a and LP21b infeasible in this configuration.
During transmission, unintentional coupling between LP21a and LP21b may occur due to fiber imperfections and perturbations, potentially causing partial energy leakage. To mitigate this, we inserted a polarization controller before the demultiplexer to suppress coupling and retain more energy in the LP21a component.
In contrast, when the multiplexer is specifically designed to excite both LP21a and LP21b modes simultaneously, the system enables full joint detection at the receiver. As shown in the supplementary experiment added in response to Comment 5(a), we constructed 4-mode and 5-mode devices that excited both degenerate LP21 modes, allowing coherent joint reception without additional polarization controller. These configurations more fully align with the reviewer’s recommended approach and demonstrate its performance benefits.

In our experiments, different MIMO-DSP dimensions were adopted according to the specific number of spatial channels involved in each transmission scenario, which include spatial modes and polarizations. Specifically, 8*8 MIMO-DSP was applied in our main transmission experiments involving four spatial modes: LP01, LP11a, LP11b, and LP21a, each with two orthogonal polarizations (4 modes * 2 polarizations = 8 spatial channels). This configuration reflects the actual multiplexed channels in the system and requires full 8*8 equalization for proper mode demultiplexing and polarization tracking.
The 10*10 MIMO-DSP was used in extended experiments where we included both degenerate LP21 modes (LP21a, LP21b), resulting in 5 modes * 2 polarizations = 10 spatial channels. This setup allowed us to evaluate the impact of including LP21b in the joint processing and confirmed its benefit in mitigating inter-modal interference.
The 3*3 MIMO-DSP was used in the U-band few-mode multiplexed transmission experiment based on IMDD. In this setup, three spatial modes (LP01, LP11a, and LP21a) were multiplexed and transmitted. Since only a single polarization state was used for each spatial mode in this IMDD-based experiment, the total number of spatial channels was three, leading to the use of a 3*3 MIMO equalization structure.

6. I notice that only 20-km transmission reach could be achieved (above the FEC limit) in the experiment using 8*8 MIMO-DSP. It’s much less than a typical strongly-coupled MDM transmission reach. please analyze it. Dos the limit come from the MPLC device?
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable question regarding the transmission distance in our experiment. We acknowledge that the 20-km reach achieved in our 8*8 MIMO-DSP experiment (while remaining above the FEC threshold) is indeed shorter than typical transmission distances reported for strongly-coupled MDM systems.
The limitation in transmission distance does not stem from the device itself. Our device exhibits low insertion loss, excellent mode selectivity and stable performance throughout our experiments. The current restriction arises primarily from algorithmic trade-offs in our DSP implementation. Since this work focuses on validating the multiplexer’s feasibility, we prioritized functional demonstration over long-haul optimization. Thus, parameters such as filter tap count and convergence behavior were optimized for practicality rather than maximal reach.
In our experimental configuration, the 8*8 MIMO-DSP system with 90 taps was employed for channel equalization. To evaluate the relationship between tap count and bit error rate (BER), we quantified BER performance across all four mode channels (at 1550 nm) under varying tap configurations. As illustrated in Figure R3, a consistent inverse correlation was observed between tap count and BER, wherein increasing the number of taps progressively reduced BER values across all mode channels. Notably, at 240 taps, all four mode channels achieved BER values below the HD-FEC threshold (BER < 3.8*10^-3), with further asymptotic improvements beyond this point.
Figure R3. The BER values of four mode channels at a wavelength of 1550 nm with different number of taps.
For long-haul transmission, signal degradation results from the combined effects of: (1) accumulated inter-modal crosstalk over longer fiber spans, (2) OSNR degradation due to multi-stage optical amplification and (3) nonlinear impairments induced by fiber nonlinearity. With deeper MIMO equalizer optimization (e.g., increased taps and advanced nonlinear compensation), our system could support extended distances while retaining the current multiplexer.

The authors have replied all the comments. But I do not think that all the modifications are satisfying.
1. The authors have explained some details of the “wide-spectrum dispersion compensation mechanism”, in which the key technique point is to “establish a multi-parameter space incorporating wavelength, mode, spatial coordinates, free-space transfer functions, and the number of diffractive layers”. However, all these factors are widely considered in previous MPLC designs. So, it confirms my concerns for the innovations of the MPLC design.
2. The authors state that the main difference between the manuscript and the Ref. A (another MPLC design covering beyond-400 nm spectrum) is that they have different design objectives, specifically, two fixed wavelengths V.S. multiple wavelengths. But I do not think that this kind of optimization could be a significant innovation.
3. The authors have explained the reception method of degenerate modes. It’s said that “During transmission, unintentional coupling between LP21a and LP21b may occur due to fiber imperfections and perturbations, potentially causing partial energy leakage. To mitigate this, we inserted a polarization controller before the demultiplexer to suppress coupling and retain more energy in the LP21a component.”
However, I disagree this experimental method of applying a PC before the receiver, only detecting on of a pair of degenerate modes, and choosing the favorable results.
4. The authors have explained my questions about both the different dimensions of MIMO-DSP and the b2b modal crosstalk level. Based on the responses, I believe that the statement in the Abstract of “A 4-linearly polarized mode multiplexer ,……, achieves over 90% mode purity and mode crosstalk less than -17 dB” is misleading. There are both strongly-coupled and weakly-coupled mode-division-multiplexing schemes for FMF transmission systems. The authors’ claim of high-purity MPLC device (only the multiplexer instead of both multiplexer/demultiplexer) may mislead the readers that it achieves so excellent performance that weakly-coupled systems could be supported by the MPLC devices, which is much more difficult than those for typical strongly-coupled systems. However, the b2b modal crosstalk is high and inter-mode MIMO-DSP for strongly-coupled transmission has to be adopted. So, I suggest modifications to this statement.
Based on the above concerns, I’m sorry to say that I still think the two innovations of the manuscript including the MPLC design and the transmission experiment are not significant enough for the publication of NC.
